title: Quantum Computing for Beginners
subtitle: Qubits, gates, interference and entanglement with hands-on circuit labs, for curious kids, teens and adults
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A friendly first course on quantum computing with no maths beyond squares and multiplication. Learn bits and qubits, amplitudes and measurement, the X, H, Z and T gates, interference, circuit text, CNOT, entanglement and Bell states, Deutsch and Grover's algorithms, noise and shots, and what quantum computers are really good for. Every chapter has Python labs, and five webxdc labs run offline: a polarizer experiment and four circuit labs built on our own mobile Lilith Composer (tap gates, see live chances, copy Qiskit or OpenQASM code) with an easy Q Console. The simulation engine and the circuit text notation come from Q.js by Stewart Smith (github.com/stewdio/q.js, MIT). Includes an intuitive intro to quantum mechanics, a Qiskit chapter and an OpenQASM chapter.

chapters.title: Quantum mechanics in plain words

maps.title: The small world
links: Light | acts like | Waves and packets

summary: Everything is made of tiny things, and tiny things do not behave like baseballs. Quantum mechanics is the rulebook for the small world of atoms, electrons and light.
Three ideas carry the whole subject. Things come in packets. Before you look, a thing can be a blend of possibilities. And looking changes what you get.
You do not need to believe it blindly. You will test it with a simulated experiment about light and sunglasses, which gives a surprise that normal thinking cannot explain.

glossary.def: A small packet. Light and energy come in packets called quanta.
One packet of light.
A spreading ripple that can add up or cancel.
The direction a light wave wiggles.
You cannot know everything about a tiny thing at once.

keyPoints: Energy and light come in packets, called quanta.
Tiny things act like waves that can add or cancel.
Before you look, a thing can be a blend of possibilities.
Looking changes the result.
A photon's polarization is the easiest real qubit.

items: ELI5. Imagine the tiniest things are like shy kittens. They come in little packets, they can be curled up in two places until you look, and the moment you peek they pick one. Sunglasses show this: two crossed pairs block all light, but slip a third pair between them and some light comes back.

Start with a ball. Roll it and you know where it is and how fast it goes, always. Baseball rules are called classical physics. They work for balls, cars and planets. They fail for the really small, like an electron.

Idea one: things come in packets. You cannot pour light out like water. Light comes as little lumps called photons, and energy as small steps. The word quantum just means a packet or a step. You can have one photon or two, never one and a half.

Idea two: tiny things spread like waves. Shoot one electron at a wall with two slits and it does not pick one slit. It goes through like a wave and the two ripples meet on the other side. Over many electrons the screen shows stripes, from ripples adding and cancelling.
Stripes are interference, the same idea you will use for algorithms.

lesson.code:
# two ripples meet; phi is how far out of step they are
import math
for phi in (0, 90, 180):
    brightness = 2 * (1 + math.cos(math.radians(phi)))
    print(phi, 'degrees out of step: brightness', round(brightness, 2))

items: Idea three: looking changes things. If you place a detector at the slits to see which slit the electron used, the stripes vanish. Asking the electron a plain question forces a plain answer, and the blend is gone. That is measurement, and you met it with the qubit.

Now a test you can do with sunglasses. A polarizing filter is a tiny fence. Light that wiggles along the fence gets through, and light that wiggles across is blocked. Two filters crossed at 90 degrees block everything.
Put a third filter at 45 degrees between them, and some light comes back through! Adding a blocker let more light pass.

Normal thinking says that is impossible. Quantum thinking says each filter is a measurement. After the 45 degree filter, the photon is re-set to that direction, so it has a fair chance of passing the last filter. Open the lab and try it. A photon's direction is a perfect real-world qubit.

chapters.title: Bits, chance and why quantum is different
summary: A normal computer stores everything as bits. A bit is a tiny switch that is either 0 or 1. Photos, games and messages are all long rows of switches.
A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can be 0, 1, or a special mix of both until you look at it. Looking at it is called measuring, and it always gives a plain 0 or 1.

This is not magic and it is not faster at everything. It is a different way to compute, and for a few jobs it can be much faster. This course teaches the real ideas, and you will play with a real simulator all the way.

glossary.def: The smallest piece of information: 0 or 1.
A quantum bit. It can be in a mix of 0 and 1.
Being in a mix of states at the same time.
Looking at a qubit, which gives a plain 0 or 1.
A normal computer program that pretends to be a quantum computer.

keyPoints: A bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can be a mix of both.
n bits hold one value. n qubits need 2 to the power n numbers to describe.
Measuring always gives a plain 0 or 1.
Quantum computers help with some jobs, not everything.
We use the Q.js simulator, which runs right here.

items: ELI5. A normal computer is a row of light switches, each on or off. A quantum computer has special switches that can be a little of both until you peek, and then they pick one.
Start with a coin. Flip it and it lands heads or tails. Before you look, you do not know which. Chance describes how likely each one is. A fair coin is 50 percent heads and 50 percent tails.
A normal bit is like a coin lying flat: it is definitely heads or definitely tails. You can read it as often as you like and it never changes. Computers are built from billions of these.

A qubit is more like a coin spinning in the air. While it spins it is not heads and not tails, it is a blend. When it lands, which is when you measure, you get one clean answer. The blend only decides the chances.

Here is why people get excited. To describe 3 normal bits you write 3 digits. To describe 3 qubits you need 8 numbers, one for each possible answer. Add one qubit and you double the numbers. 50 qubits already need more numbers than any laptop can store.

A big warning, because the internet gets this wrong. A quantum computer is not trying every answer at once and handing you the best. When you measure you only get one answer. The skill is in arranging things so the right answer becomes the likely one. You will learn how.

chapters.title: The qubit: states, amplitudes and measurement
summary: A qubit state has two numbers called amplitudes, one for 0 and one for 1. Write the state as (a, b). The state |0> is (1, 0) and |1> is (0, 1).
The chance of seeing 0 is a squared, and the chance of seeing 1 is b squared. This is the Born rule. The chances must add to 1, so the state is always scaled to fit.
Measuring makes the qubit pick one answer using those chances, and afterwards it stays as that answer. The blend is gone. That is why you measure at the end of a circuit.

glossary.def: A number attached to each outcome. Squared, it is the chance.
Chance of an outcome equals its amplitude squared.
Scale a state so the chances add up to 1.
The bracket notation |0> for a state.
After measuring, the state becomes the answer you saw.

keyPoints: State (a, b): amplitude a for 0, b for 1.
Chance of 0 is a squared. Chance of 1 is b squared.
Chances add up to exactly 1.
Measuring picks one and the blend is gone.
Amplitudes can be negative. Chances never are.

items: ELI5. A qubit is a spinning coin. Its two numbers tell you how likely heads or tails is when it lands. You square the numbers to get the chances, and they always add up to one whole.
Every qubit state is described by two amplitudes. Think of them as dials. One dial is for the answer 0 and one for the answer 1. A plain 0 has the first dial full and the second at zero.

To turn amplitudes into chances you square them. If the state is (0.7071, 0.7071), the chance of 0 is 0.7071 times 0.7071, which is about 0.5. The chance of 1 is also 0.5. That is a fair coin flip. This is called the Born rule.

lesson.code:
a, b = 0.7071, 0.7071
print('chance of 0:', round(a * a, 2))
print('chance of 1:', round(b * b, 2))

items: Why square? Because amplitudes can be negative, and a chance cannot. Squaring makes every answer positive. Later you will see that the sign matters a lot, because amplitudes can cancel each other out.

Now try it yourself. The first lab in this chapter is our own Lilith Composer, powered by the Q.js engine. Tap the H gate, then tap a square on the wire. The bars show the chances. Then use the Q Console under the circuit: type H 1 and press Go.

When you run shots, each shot is one full measurement. A coin that is 50 percent heads will not give exactly half every time, just like a real coin. More shots give numbers closer to the true chances.

chapters.title: One-qubit gates: X, H, Z and T

maps.title: Gates
links: T gate | turns | Phase a little

summary: A gate is a tiny step that changes a qubit. You build a quantum program by lining gates up on a wire, like beads on a string. Time moves left to right.

X flips 0 and 1, like a NOT. H, the Hadamard, turns a plain 0 into a fair blend. Z flips the sign of the 1 amplitude, which you cannot see directly. T is a smaller sign turn, a quarter of a half-turn.
Every gate can be undone, because it is reversible. Doing X twice is a no-op, and doing H twice gets you back where you started. That is one big difference from normal logic gates.

glossary.def: A step that changes a qubit.
Makes an even blend from a plain 0 or 1.
The NOT gate: swaps the 0 and 1 amplitudes.
A hidden angle on the 1 amplitude.
Every gate can be undone.

keyPoints: X swaps the two amplitudes.
Z negates the 1 amplitude. T turns the phase by a quarter step.
H twice is the same as nothing.
Gates are reversible, unlike measuring.

items: ELI5. Gates are little moves you do to the spinning coin: flip it, spin it fair, or turn its secret direction. Every move can be undone by doing it again or the opposite way.
X is the easiest gate. It swaps the two amplitudes. A plain 0 becomes a plain 1 and a plain 1 becomes a plain 0. Think of it as a flip switch.

H, called the Hadamard gate, is the star. Give it a plain 0 and it makes an equal blend. Measure that and you get a fair coin flip. In Q.js you write it as H. This is how you make your first superposition.

Z does not change the chances of a plain 0 or 1, so it looks like nothing happens. What it does is flip the sign of the 1 amplitude. The sign is called phase. You cannot see it directly, but it changes what the next gate does.

lesson.code:
# the gates as number pairs
def x(s): return [s[1], s[0]]
def z(s): return [s[0], -s[1]]
r = 0.7071
def h(s): return [r * (s[0] + s[1]), r * (s[0] - s[1])]
print(h([1, 0]))
print(h(h([1, 0])))

items: Look at that last line. H followed by H returns to the start. The second H cancels the first. This is the hint of something deeper that you will meet in the next chapter.
Tip: in the editor each column is one moment in time and each row is one qubit. You can type circuits in the Q Console too: H 1 adds an H on qubit 1 in the next free column.

chapters.title: Interference: the real power
summary: Amplitudes are like waves. Two waves that line up make a bigger wave. Two waves that are opposite cancel out to nothing. Quantum computers use exactly this.
When two paths lead to the same answer, you add their amplitudes first, and then square. Same sign gives a bigger chance, called constructive interference. Opposite signs cancel, called destructive.
That is the whole trick behind quantum speedups: use phases so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer grows. A coin cannot do this, because ordinary chances only add.

glossary.def: Amplitudes adding or cancelling.
Same sign: the chance grows.
Opposite sign: the chance shrinks.
The sign or angle of an amplitude.
One route a qubit could take to an answer.

keyPoints: Add amplitudes, then square.
Same sign grows. Opposite sign cancels.
H, then Z, then H turns 0 into 1.
H, then T, then H gives an in-between chance.
Quantum speedups come from steering interference.

items: ELI5. Waves can team up or cancel, like two kids pushing a swing in time or against each other. Quantum tricks time the pushes so the wrong answers cancel and the right answer swings high.
Here is the experiment of the chapter. Start with a plain 0. Apply H to make a blend. Apply H again. The qubit returns to a plain 0 every time. Nothing random happened at all.

That is strange. After the first H you had a fair coin. A fair coin flipped by another fair coin should still be random. The reason it is not: the two paths to the answer 1 have opposite signs and cancel, and the two paths to 0 add up.

Now put a Z between the two H gates. Z flips a sign, so now the paths to 0 cancel and the paths to 1 add up. H then Z then H turns a plain 0 into a plain 1 with certainty. The phase is the steering wheel.

lesson.code:
# H, then a phase turn of phi, then H
import math
for phi in (0, 90, 180):
    p1 = math.sin(math.radians(phi) / 2) ** 2
    print(phi, 'degrees gives chance of 1:', round(p1, 2))

items: With a phase of 0 you get 0 percent, with 180 degrees you get 100 percent, and with 90 degrees you get 50 percent. A phase of 180 degrees is exactly a Z gate. The T gate is 45 degrees. Try these in the labs.
This is why quantum computing needs careful design. You cannot just throw gates at a problem. You line up phases so that the wrong answers cancel. The next chapters build real examples.

chapters.title: Reading circuits and the text syntax

maps.title: Circuits
links: X#0 and X#1 | make | A CNOT

summary: A quantum circuit is a grid. Each row is one qubit and each column is one moment in time. A gate sits where a row and a column meet. An empty spot is the identity, written I, which does nothing.
Q.js lets you write a circuit as plain text. Gates in a row are joined with a dash, and rows are on separate lines. So H-X-I on one line means H, then X, then nothing.
To link two qubits you tag gates with #. X#0 is the control and X#1 is its target, together a CNOT. Typing circuits as text is quick and easy to share.

glossary.def: A grid of gates on qubit wires.
One column: things that happen at the same time.
A gate that does nothing.
The qubit that decides if the gate happens.
The qubit that gets changed.

keyPoints: Rows are qubits. Columns are moments.
I is a gate that does nothing.
Separate gates in a row with a dash.
X#0 and X#1 in one column form a CNOT.
The Q Console builds circuits with commands such as H 1.

items: ELI5. A circuit is a music sheet: each line is a player and each beat is a moment. You read it from left to right, and a blank spot is a rest, written I.
Look at a circuit like a music sheet. The rows are instruments and the columns are beats. All gates in one column happen together. Moving to the next column moves time forward.

That is a 2 qubit circuit. The first line is qubit 1 and the second is qubit 2. In the first moment qubit 1 gets an H. In the second moment qubit 1 gets an X. The third moment has nothing for qubit 1 and an H for qubit 2.
To make a CNOT, put X#0 on the control row and X#1 on the target row, in the same column. The CNOT flips the target only when the control is 1. Next chapter explains why it is special.
You do not have to type this by hand. In the Q Console you can type H 1 and then CNOT 1 2, and the console writes the text for you. Type text to see it. The same text can go back into the editor.
Practice by reading. Every circuit you meet from now on is just this grid, so you can always tell what it does by reading left to right.

summary: Two qubits have four possible answers: 00, 01, 10 and 11. So a two qubit state is four amplitudes. In Q.js the left bit is qubit 1.
If the qubits are separate, you can build the four amplitudes by multiplying: the tensor product. A, B gives a0 b0, a0 b1, a1 b0 and a1 b1. A state you can build this way is called a product state.
The CNOT gate links two qubits. If the control is 1, it flips the target. If the control is 0, nothing happens. With H plus CNOT you can make states that are not product states.

glossary.def: Multiplying amplitudes to combine separate qubits.
A state of separate, unlinked qubits.
Flips the target if the control is 1.
A plain state such as 01.
The qubit that decides whether the target flips.

keyPoints: Two qubits have 4 amplitudes, one per answer.
Tensor product: multiply the amplitudes.
CNOT swaps the amplitudes of 10 and 11.
A state is a product if a0*d equals b*c for amplitudes a, b, c, d.
Not every two qubit state is a product.

items: ELI5. Two coins can be glued so that one flips only when the other shows heads. That glue gate is called CNOT, and it is how coins start talking to each other.
One qubit has two answers, 0 and 1. Two qubits have four, written 00, 01, 10 and 11. The first digit is qubit 1. A state needs one amplitude for each, so four numbers. Three qubits would need eight.

If you set two qubits up separately, you can find the combined state by multiplying. Qubit 1 is (a0, a1) and qubit 2 is (b0, b1). The combined amplitudes are a0 times b0, a0 times b1, a1 times b0 and a1 times b1. This is the tensor product.

lesson.code:
def tensor(a, b):
    return [a[0]*b[0], a[0]*b[1], a[1]*b[0], a[1]*b[1]]
print(tensor([1, 0], [0, 1]))   # 0 and 1 gives 01
print(tensor([0.7071, 0.7071], [1, 0]))

items: The CNOT gate has two inputs. If the control qubit is 0, it does nothing. If the control is 1, it flips the target. On the four amplitudes, that means the answers 10 and 11 swap. The other two stay.
Try it by typing in the console of the next chapter: new 2, then X 1, then CNOT 1 2, then run. You should see 11. The CNOT copied the 1 from qubit 1 onto qubit 2.
Everything so far could be done by separate qubits. The next chapter shows how H and CNOT together make something new: the qubits can no longer be pulled apart.

chapters.title: Entanglement and Bell states

maps.title: Entanglement
links: H then CNOT | makes | Bell state
Measure one | tells you | The other

summary: Entanglement is when qubits are linked so tightly that you cannot describe one without the others. The famous recipe: put H on qubit 1, then a CNOT from 1 to 2.
The result is the Bell state. It is half 00 and half 11. Measure it and you get 00 or 11, each 50 percent of the time, never 01 or 10. Each qubit alone is a fair coin, but the two coins always agree.
Entanglement does not send messages faster than light. The results look random to each side. You only see the link when you compare them afterwards.

glossary.def: Qubits linked so they cannot be described separately.
The two-qubit entangled state made with H and CNOT.
Outcomes that agree or match.
A three-qubit entangled state: all 0 or all 1.
A state that is not entangled.

keyPoints: H on qubit 1, then CNOT 1 to 2, makes a Bell state.
Bell outcomes: 00 or 11, 50 percent each.
Each qubit alone looks like a fair coin.
The two coins always agree.
No message is sent: the results are random until compared.

items: ELI5. Two magic coins can always agree even though each one alone is random, like twins who always pick the same ice cream without talking. That is entanglement, but it cannot be used as a phone.

Here is the recipe. Start with two plain 0 qubits. Put an H on qubit 1. Now qubit 1 is a blend. Add a CNOT with qubit 1 as the control and qubit 2 as the target. The control is a blend, so the target is a blend too, and they are tied together.
The state is now half 00 and half 11. If you measure qubit 1 and see 0, qubit 2 will be 0. If you see 1, qubit 2 will be 1. Each coin alone is perfectly random, yet the two always agree.

This cannot be a product state. A product state has a0 times d equal to b times c. Here the amplitudes are 0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071. The first times the last is 0.5, but the middle two give 0. They do not match, so this state is entangled.

Time for the lab in the practice section. Solve the levels: copy a bit with CNOT, make a Bell pair, make the opposite pair, and build a three-qubit GHZ state. In the Q Console you can type new 3, H 1, CNOT 1 2, CNOT 2 3 and explain.

One more myth to bust. Entanglement is not a phone line. If you are far away from your friend and you measure your qubit, you see a random result. It only shows a pattern when you later compare results. That is why it cannot send messages.

chapters.title: Small algorithms: Deutsch and Grover

maps.title: Algorithms
links: One query | is enough | For Deutsch
Grover | needs | About root N steps

summary: An oracle is a black box that hides a secret function. Deutsch's problem: is the hidden rule constant (same answer for both inputs) or balanced (different answers)? A normal computer must ask twice. A quantum circuit can ask once.

Grover's search finds a marked item in an unsorted list of N items. A normal computer needs about N over 2 tries on average. Grover needs about the square root of N steps. For a million items that is about a thousand steps instead of half a million.
Both use the interference you learned: the oracle marks the answer with a phase, and the other gates make wrong answers cancel and the right one grow.

glossary.def: A black box that holds a secret rule.
Gives the same answer for every input.
Gives 0 for half the inputs and 1 for the other half.
A quantum search that takes about the square root of N steps.
Fewer steps needed than the best normal way.

keyPoints: Deutsch: one oracle query tells constant from balanced.
Grover: about the square root of N steps for N items.
Both mark answers with a phase and interfere.
Grover's speedup is quadratic, not magic.
You can build 2 qubit Grover in the lab.

items: ELI5. Deutsch asks a secret box one question instead of two. Grover finds a hidden prize by making the right box a little brighter every round, like turning up a dimmer.

Imagine a secret rule that takes a 0 or a 1 and gives back a 0 or a 1. There are four possible rules. Two are constant: always 0 or always 1. Two are balanced: copy the input, or flip it. You must find out which kind it is.

A normal computer must ask the rule twice, once for 0 and once for 1, to compare the answers. Deutsch's circuit asks once. It puts the input in a blend, asks the oracle, and then lets the two paths interfere. If the rule is constant the answer is 0, if balanced the answer is 1.

lesson.code:
def deutsch(f0, f1):
    a0 = ((-1) ** f0 + (-1) ** f1) / 2
    p0 = a0 * a0
    return 'constant' if p0 > 0.5 else 'balanced'
print(deutsch(0, 0), deutsch(0, 1))

items: Grover's search is the more useful one. Take 4 hidden boxes and one of them has a prize. A normal computer checks boxes one at a time. Grover starts with an even blend of all boxes, marks the prize with a phase, and then does a reflection that makes the prized box more likely.

For 4 items one round makes the prize certain. For larger lists you repeat the round about pi over 4 times the square root of N times. Do too few rounds and the prize is not yet likely. Do too many and it fades again. It rotates like a clock hand.

lesson.code:
import math
N = 16
k = int(math.pi / 4 * math.sqrt(N))
print('rounds:', k)
theta = math.asin(1 / math.sqrt(N))
print('chance of prize:', round(math.sin((2 * k + 1) * theta) ** 2, 3))

items: Nobody gets to skip checking. Real Grover circuits include an oracle and a flip around the average. The lab gives you ready circuits to experiment with so you can see the answer rise.

chapters.title: Noise, shots and real hardware
summary: Real quantum chips are fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals disturb qubits and make mistakes. This is noise, and the loss of the quantum blend is called decoherence. Many chips work near absolute zero.

Because one measurement gives one random answer, you run the circuit many times. Each run is a shot. A hundred shots show you the chances roughly, a thousand show more. The error shrinks with the square root of the shots.

A normal computer can simulate a quantum one, but it needs 2 to the n numbers. Around 30 qubits fills a normal PC and around 50 fills a supercomputer. That is exactly why real hardware is interesting.

glossary.def: One run of the circuit with one measurement.
Unwanted disturbance that causes errors.
The qubit losing its quantum blend.
Using many noisy qubits to make one reliable one.
How far a measured chance is likely to be from the true one.

keyPoints: A shot is one run and one measurement.
Estimates improve with the square root of the shots.
Noise and decoherence cause errors.
Error correction needs many extra qubits.
Simulating n qubits needs 2^n numbers.

items: ELI5. Real quantum computers are shy and wobbly, so we repeat the test many times and count what we see, the way you roll a die often to learn if it is fair.

When you ran 100 shots earlier, you noticed that the Bell state did not give exactly 50 and 50. That is not a bug. Each shot is one random measurement, like a coin flip, so the totals wobble around the true chances.

How big is the wobble? About the square root of p times one minus p, divided by the square root of shots. For a fair coin and 100 shots that is about 0.05, or 5 percent. For 10,000 shots it is 0.005. To be 10 times more accurate you need 100 times more shots.

lesson.code:
shots = 100
p = 0.5
err = (p * (1 - p) / shots) ** 0.5
print('standard error:', round(err, 3))

items: On real hardware the picture is messier. Gates are not perfect, qubits slowly lose their blend, and measurement can read the wrong answer. Today's machines have dozens to hundreds of noisy qubits, and engineers are working on error correction.

Error correction spreads one reliable qubit across many noisy ones, similar to how you repeat a message three times so one smudge does not matter. It is a big engineering goal, and useful big machines need it.

Finally, why a simulator is limited. Every qubit you add doubles the memory. At 16 bytes per number, 30 qubits need 16 gigabytes. 40 qubits need 16 terabytes. That is why Q.js is great for learning on small circuits, but real chips are needed for large ones.

chapters.title: From the composer to real code: OpenQASM and Qiskit
summary: Every circuit you drew has a text form. The Code panel under the composer shows it as Qiskit, an open source Python toolkit from IBM, and as OpenQASM, a plain text format many tools read.
In Qiskit you make a QuantumCircuit and call methods like h, x and cx. A Statevector gives you the exact chances, and a Sampler runs shots on a simulator or a real chip.
Watch one trap: Qiskit counts qubits from 0 and prints qubit 0 on the right, while our composer reads q[0] at the top and writes it on the left.

glossary.def: An open source Python toolkit for quantum circuits.
The Qiskit object that holds your gates.
A plain text language for circuits.
Runs a circuit many times and returns counts.
Rewrite a circuit to use the gates a chip supports.

keyPoints: qc = QuantumCircuit(2) makes 2 qubits.
qc.h(0) is an H on qubit 0. qc.cx(0, 1) is a CNOT.
Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict() gives exact chances.
Qiskit prints qubit 0 on the right.
OpenQASM 3 is the shared text format.

items: ELI5. The composer draws your circuit, and the code panel writes the same thing as words, like a drawing and its caption. Qiskit is one language for it and OpenQASM is another.

Open any lab and the Code panel below the composer. Build the Bell state with H then CNOT and open Qiskit. You will see a few lines of Python. The composer did not invent the code. It just translated your picture.

lesson.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict())

items: Line by line. The first line makes a circuit with 2 qubits, both starting at 0. The H puts qubit 0 in a blend. The CNOT links qubit 1 to it. Statevector works out the chances exactly with no shots, like our bars. The output shows 00 and 11 with 0.5 each.

Next is the trap. Our composer reads left to right, so q[0] is the leftmost bit. Qiskit does the opposite and writes qubit 0 on the right. A state we call 10 appears in Qiskit as 01. The result is the same, only the label is flipped, so always check which one you are reading.

OpenQASM is the same circuit as plain text. Many tools can read it, so it works like a shared language. To run on a real chip, you make a free IBM Quantum account, pick a machine, and the toolkit transpiles your circuit into the gates that chip supports. Queues can take a while, so simulate first.

A good habit: draw it in the composer, look at the Qiskit code, change one line, and predict what changes. Then try the code in a notebook. Reading code that you drew yourself is a gentle way into real quantum programming.

chapters.title: OpenQASM: the shared language of circuits
summary: OpenQASM stands for Open Quantum Assembly Language. It writes a circuit as plain lines of text, one gate per line. IBM Quantum Composer, Qiskit and many other tools can read and write it.
A program has a header, a place to declare qubits, a list of gates and a measurement. Every line ends with a semicolon. Comments start with two slashes.
Version 3 is the modern one and the composer shows it. Older files use version 2, with slightly different words, and you can convert them by hand.

glossary.def: Open Quantum Assembly Language: plain text for circuits.
The first lines: version and the gate library.
The standard gate library: h, x, y, z, t, cx, cz and more.
A line that makes qubits or bits, like qubit[2] q;
Reads qubits into classical bits.

keyPoints: Start with OPENQASM 3.0; and include stdgates.inc.
qubit[2] q; makes two qubits. bit[2] c; makes two result bits.
h q[0]; is an H on the first qubit. cx q[0], q[1]; is a CNOT.
c = measure q; reads all qubits into bits.
Version 2 used qreg, creg and measure q -> c.

items: ELI5. OpenQASM is a recipe card for a circuit: one line for each move, written in a language every quantum machine can read. You can mail it to a friend and they can run your exact circuit.

Think of OpenQASM as the recipe card for a circuit. The picture in the composer and the card say exactly the same thing. The advantage of text is that you can save it, mail it, paste it into other tools or run it on a real machine.

Read it top down. The first line names the version. The include line brings in the standard gates, so h, x and cx mean what you expect. The qubit line makes two qubits called q, numbered from 0. The bit line makes two classical bits called c to hold the answers.

Then come the gates, one per line, in the order they happen. A gate name, a space, then the qubits it acts on. h q[0]; is an H on qubit 0. cx q[0], q[1]; is a CNOT with qubit 0 as control and qubit 1 as target. The last line measures every qubit into the bits.

Here is how our composer symbols map to the text. H is h, X is x, Y is y, Z is z, T is t, CNOT is cx and CZ is cz. Each column of the composer becomes a few lines, in order from left to right. Open the Code panel on the OpenQASM tab and watch it change as you tap.

You will meet older version 2 files. They say qreg and creg instead of qubit and bit, include a library called qelib1.inc, and measure with an arrow. The gates are the same. Converting between the two is mostly renaming a few lines.

Version 3 adds extras that you will grow into. You can define your own gate, like a recipe that calls other gates. You can run a gate only if a measured bit is 1, which is how teleportation works. And you can write angles for rotation gates, like rz(pi/4) q[0]; which is a smaller phase turn.

practice.intro: Write parse_gate(line): turn 'cx q[0], q[1];' into ['cx', [0, 1]] and 'h q[2];' into ['h', [2]].
practice.hint: Split off the name, then dig the numbers out of the brackets.
practice.solution:
def parse_gate(line):
    line = line.strip().rstrip(';')
    name, rest = line.split(' ', 1)
    qs = []
    for p in rest.split(','):
        qs.append(int(p.strip().split('[')[1].split(']')[0]))
    return [name, qs]

chapters.title: Uses, myths and where to go next
summary: Quantum computers are expected to help with a few kinds of problems: simulating molecules and materials, searching, and breaking some codes. Shor's algorithm can factor large numbers much faster than known normal methods.

That is why people are building new codes that resist quantum attacks. Everyday tasks like browsing, email, games and spreadsheets will not get faster. Quantum computers are co-processors for special jobs.
To keep going: play with Q.js, try IBM Quantum and other free cloud services, follow Qiskit and Cirq tutorials, and read about the linear algebra under the hood. You already know the key ideas.

keyPoints: Shor factors big numbers quickly.
Grover gives a square root speedup for search.
Chemistry and materials are natural uses.
A quantum computer will not speed up everyday apps.
Keep learning with simulators and cloud tools.

items: ELI5. Quantum computers will be special helpers for chemistry and secret codes, not faster game consoles. They are more like a telescope than a faster bicycle.

What could a large reliable quantum computer do? The most natural job is simulating nature, because nature is quantum. That might mean better batteries, medicines and fertilizers. A normal computer struggles because the numbers double with every particle.

Shor's algorithm factors a large number into primes. Today's internet security often relies on factoring being hard. A big enough quantum computer would break some of it. The reply is new encryption that quantum computers cannot break, and it is already being rolled out.

The code above factors by trying every divisor. It is fine for small numbers and hopeless for numbers hundreds of digits long. Shor's trick is to find a repeating pattern using interference, and from the pattern it works out the factors.
Common myths. A quantum computer does not try every answer at once and pick the best. It is not a faster laptop. It cannot send messages faster than light. And it is not here to replace your phone.

You now know qubits, amplitudes, gates, interference, entanglement and a little of two algorithms. Keep playing. Build a circuit, guess the result before you run it, and see if you were right. That is how real quantum programmers learn.
